focus_question: How do data, learning, and machine limits shape a deployable ML system?
description: Follow mechanisms from training data and learned behavior through execution, measurement, release, and operational feedback. Chapter highlights locate the teaching evidence; arrows are draft propositions with stated conditions.
title: How do data, learning, and machine limits shape a deployable ML system?

nodes.label: Training data
nodes.summary: Examples used to fit model parameters; their coverage and labels help determine learned behavior.
nodes.claim: Training data plus the optimization procedure produce the program, so changing the dataset changes system behavior as surely as changing source code, and debugging, versioning, and review must extend to the data.

nodes.label: Learned behavior
nodes.summary: The predictions a trained model produces on inputs, whose usefulness and physical deliverability must both be established.
nodes.claim: Every ML system must show both that its learned behavior is trustworthy and that the machine delivers it within time, memory, energy, and cost budgets, so an accurate but slow model and a fast model trained on unrepresentative data are both failures.

nodes.label: Execution time
nodes.summary: Time spent moving data, performing arithmetic, and paying system overhead; the applicable overlap model depends on the execution boundary.
nodes.claim: Across Data, Algorithm, and Machine, execution time factors as samples per task times FLOPs per sample times seconds per FLOP (where the first two multiply to total operations O), and unpacks on hardware into bytes moved over bandwidth plus operations over peak rate times utilization plus fixed overhead, with ideal overlap giving the larger of the first two plus overhead, so a faster component helps only through the share of time it changes.

nodes.label: Memory capacity
nodes.summary: The amount of resident model and runtime state a machine can hold; fitting is a feasibility condition before speed is considered.
nodes.claim: Each tier's hardware offers a peak compute rate, a memory bandwidth, and a fixed overhead that enter the iron law's three terms, while memory capacity and energy act as feasibility preconditions that can rule a tier out before any term is evaluated.

nodes.label: Power budget
nodes.summary: The allowed rate of energy consumption, limited by battery supply and heat dissipation.
nodes.claim: On untethered devices energy per inference is first-order with two distinct limits, a battery budget fixable by duty cycling or a lighter model and a thermal ceiling on sustained power that throttles regardless of charge, and transmitting raw data can cost more energy than inferring locally.

nodes.label: Data locality
nodes.summary: Placing computation near the data when transfer delay or bandwidth makes remote execution infeasible.
nodes.claim: A remote path is rejected when even its lower bound (transfer time plus propagation plus remote compute) exceeds the deadline, because transmission and propagation cannot be bought down with more remote compute, and only surviving paths are compared on measured time.

nodes.label: System requirements
nodes.summary: Operationally measurable targets and constraints that determine what counts as a successful system.
nodes.claim: A request becomes a requirement only when stated as a measurable improvement over a named baseline and decomposed into statistical, physical, and operational constraints bound before development, because a metric that diverges from the goal defeats the system before training starts.

nodes.label: Stage interface contract
nodes.summary: A checked specification of the inputs, outputs, and invariants at a pipeline boundary.
nodes.claim: Each stage has an input contract, an output contract, and a quality invariant, and enforcing them at the boundaries turns the feedback loop into an audit that names which upstream stage owns a defect.

nodes.label: Release gate
nodes.summary: A decision that blocks deployment unless a particular artifact meets declared evaluation thresholds.
nodes.claim: Evaluation measures and validation decides: a release needs evidence on latency, subgroup performance, calibration, robustness across sites and time, and operational readiness, recorded in an immutable manifest, and a failed threshold routes the fix to the stage that owns it.

nodes.label: Labels
nodes.summary: Supervision targets that specify the behavior the model is trained to reproduce.
nodes.claim: Ground truth is the system's specification, so a labeling error becomes part of the definition of correct; labeling usually dominates data cost, granularity sets per-label cost, and label quality is bounded through chance-corrected agreement, gold checks, and monitoring of agreement over time.

nodes.label: Data leakage
nodes.summary: Information crossing training, validation, or test boundaries so evaluation ceases to estimate generalization.
nodes.claim: Train, validation, and test sets are trust boundaries, and leakage occurs when information crosses them through duplicates, split groups, future-derived features, or preprocessing fitted before the split, so splits are group-keyed, transforms are fit on train only, and features use point-in-time retrieval.

nodes.label: Input pipeline
nodes.summary: The storage, decoding, transformation, and transfer stages that deliver usable examples to the accelerator.
nodes.claim: Training throughput is the minimum of the compute-limited rate and the data supply rate, and storage bandwidth, host decode, and bytes per sample each impose a slowest-stage bound, so the input path is sized for the rate the accelerator consumes.

nodes.label: Training-serving parity
nodes.summary: Agreement between the feature values produced by training and serving transformations for the same raw request.
nodes.claim: Shared feature code is not enough: fitted state (normalization constants, vocabularies, gain handling) must be fitted once on the training split, persisted with the model, and replayed identically at serving, because a skewed feature is still a valid vector and raises no error; a violation is training-serving skew, an internal divergence of logic or state that differs from drift in the environment.

nodes.label: Matrix multiplication
nodes.teaches: Network as linear maps and nonlinearities
nodes.summary: A shared arithmetic primitive for dense layers and lowered neural-network operations.
nodes.claim: A layer is one matrix product plus bias followed by an element-wise activation and a network is their composition, without the nonlinearity the stack collapses to one linear map, and inference runs only the forward pass while training adds loss, backward pass, and update.
nodes.concept: Network as linear maps and nonlinearities

nodes.label: Saved activations
nodes.summary: Forward intermediate tensors retained because backward derivative rules need their values.
nodes.claim: Backpropagation applies the chain rule layer by layer in reverse, each dense layer needs two backward products of forward size, so a training step costs about three times the forward matrix work and every forward activation must stay live, or be recomputed, until the backward pass reaches its layer.

nodes.label: Parameter gradients
nodes.summary: Derivatives of training loss with respect to parameters, used to update those parameters.
nodes.claim: Cross-entropy against a one-hot label reduces to the negative log of the correct-class probability, its fused softmax gradient is p minus y, and mini-batch gradient descent averages per-example gradients so the batch size becomes the main systems knob.

nodes.label: Training state
nodes.teaches: Training holds four kinds of state
nodes.summary: Resident weights, saved activations, gradients, and optimizer state required during training.
nodes.claim: Training memory is weights plus gradients plus optimizer state plus saved activations, while inference keeps only the weights and the largest adjacent pair of activation buffers, and raising the batch leaves parameter state fixed while multiplying saved activations.
nodes.concept: Training holds four kinds of state

nodes.label: Inductive bias
nodes.teaches: Inductive bias buys data and cost
nodes.summary: A structural assumption encoded by an architecture that restricts its hypothesis space and changes learning and execution costs.
nodes.claim: Each architecture is defined by a structural assumption fixed before training (locality and weight sharing, ordered recurrence, content-based routing), and a bias that matches the data cuts parameters, samples, and operations while weak priors pay off only at large data and compute.
nodes.concept: Inductive bias buys data and cost

nodes.label: Self-attention
nodes.summary: An operation that lets tokens combine information from other positions; dense score computation grows quadratically with sequence length.
nodes.claim: Dense self-attention computes sequence-length-squared score interactions, so doubling context quadruples that work, while materializing the score matrix is optional storage that tiled kernels remove, and attention arithmetic dominates a block only past a context of about six times the hidden size.

nodes.label: Reverse-mode autodiff
nodes.summary: A reverse traversal that computes parameter gradients from a scalar loss using recorded forward operations.
nodes.claim: Reverse mode propagates adjoints as vector-Jacobian products from a scalar loss and yields every gradient in one backward sweep at a small constant multiple of forward cost, never materializing a Jacobian, at the price of a recorded graph and retained forward values.

nodes.label: Dispatch overhead
nodes.summary: Host-side work paid to submit operations; many short kernels can make it dominate device execution.
nodes.claim: Each eagerly dispatched operation pays a fixed host cost of microseconds, so a workload of many small kernels is overhead-bound when total dispatch time exceeds device time, while large GEMM-dominated layers are device-bound; compilation, fusion, larger batches, and graph replay are the levers.

nodes.label: Kernel fusion
nodes.summary: Combining operations to reduce dispatches and keep intermediate values in local storage when dependencies and resource limits permit.
nodes.claim: Most elementwise and normalization operators are memory-bound, so fusing a chain of k of them into one kernel cuts idealized traffic from 2kNb to 2Nb and removes k-1 launches, but a compiler fuses only what it sees together and fusion cannot drop values a backward rule must read.

nodes.label: Time to target quality
nodes.summary: Elapsed training time needed to reach a stated quality threshold, coupling convergence work with achieved execution rate.
nodes.claim: In the macroscopic D·A·M product form of the iron law, training work is about 6PD FLOPs (D tokens times 6P FLOPs per token) and run time is that work over peak rate times utilization, so every point of utilization recovered at constant power removes time, energy, and dollars in the same proportion, while memory sits outside the law as a feasibility gate.

nodes.label: Model FLOPs utilization
nodes.summary: Achieved model arithmetic divided by the relevant peak arithmetic rate; useful work differs from device busy time.
nodes.claim: MFU is useful model FLOPs per step over peak times measured step time and is the honest estimate of utilization, whereas the busy time a device monitor reports is only an upper bound, high for a memory-stalled job and low for a data-starved one.

nodes.label: Activation checkpointing
nodes.summary: Retaining selected forward tensors and recomputing discarded intermediates during backward to reduce activation memory.
nodes.claim: Activation checkpointing recomputes segment interiors to cut activation memory from O(L) to O(sqrt L) for about one extra forward pass, and gradient accumulation builds a large effective batch from micro-batches that fit, reproducing the large-batch gradient only when losses are normalized consistently.

nodes.label: Selection overhead
nodes.summary: The time or resource cost of scoring and filtering examples before or during training.
nodes.claim: A training-time claim for data selection holds only if selection time plus subset training time is less than full training time at matched quality and coverage, so scorer size and refresh rate, not the retained fraction, decide whether selection is a net saving.

nodes.label: Training subset
nodes.summary: Selected examples retained for training, whose value must be checked against quality and coverage constraints.
nodes.claim: Deduplication, quality pruning, and coreset selection shrink training work before training, but a score ranking must be constrained by per-class or per-slice coverage floors, which carry an explicit opportunity cost and can make a budget infeasible.

nodes.label: Model-data allocation
nodes.summary: Allocation of a fixed training compute budget between parameter count and training data within a fitted scaling regime.
nodes.claim: Controlled sweeps fit a compute-optimal balance of about 20 tokens per parameter, so a run whose unique tokens per parameter sit well below it is data-starved and repeats its corpus, which is the regime where selection rather than more compute moves the run toward the frontier.

nodes.label: Quantization
nodes.summary: Representing tensors at lower precision to reduce storage and traffic, subject to quality and runtime support.
nodes.claim: Accuracy holds on a plateau down to some bit width and then falls off a model-dependent cliff, so post-training quantization over a calibration set comes first and quantization-aware training is spent only when it misses the quality target.

nodes.label: Weight sparsity
nodes.summary: Zero-valued or removed weights whose storage and execution benefit depends on pattern, metadata, and sparse kernels.
nodes.claim: Pruning removes the weights or structures with the smallest loss impact, but only structured removal (channels, heads, layers, or 2:4 groups) yields smaller dense or hardware-supported tensors, and scattered zeros saved in a dense tensor save nothing.

nodes.label: Tiling
nodes.summary: Partitioning operations so operand blocks can be reused in local memory rather than repeatedly fetched from off-chip memory.
nodes.claim: Tiling partitions an operation into blocks that fit a fast memory tier so each block is reused before eviction, with tile size bounded by every live buffer and dimensions off the tile grid paying a fringe penalty.

nodes.label: Operand reuse
nodes.summary: Using a locally retained operand for multiple arithmetic operations before fetching it again.
nodes.claim: Every matmul operand is reused along a different loop and local storage can hold only one cheaply, so the loop order decides which operand stays (weight-, output-, or input-stationary) and two identical schedules can differ many-fold in traffic.

nodes.label: Accelerated fraction
nodes.summary: The fraction of baseline end-to-end time that an optimization can accelerate; the remaining time limits total gain.
nodes.claim: Acceleration speeds only the fraction p of baseline time on the accelerated path, so speedup is 1/((1-p) + p/A) and never exceeds 1/(1-p), and the unaccelerated fraction is defined by the intervention (data loading, host overhead, unsupported operators, launches).

nodes.label: Benchmark protocol
nodes.summary: The workload, software, hardware, measurement boundary, and run rules required to interpret and reproduce a result.
nodes.claim: A claim becomes testable only when the benchmark fixes the input and output boundary, a quality floor, the model and runtime, the metrics, an open-loop synchronized harness, and recorded run rules, and a number reported without them cannot be reproduced or refuted.

nodes.label: Model quality
nodes.summary: Task-relevant predictive performance evaluated over appropriate distributions and subgroups, with uncertainty.
nodes.claim: Compression and deployment can leave top-1 accuracy nearly unchanged while degrading calibration and accuracy on rare slices, so a model is accepted against absolute gates set in advance (aggregate accuracy, calibration error, deployment-critical slices).

nodes.label: Latency SLO
nodes.summary: A target for the fraction of requests completing within a stated latency boundary.
nodes.claim: Mean latency hides the tail, so serving benchmarks report percentiles under a stated offered load and judge them against an SLO (a target for a named indicator, distinct from a contractual SLA), and generative workloads report time to first token and time per output token together.

nodes.label: Distribution shift
nodes.summary: A change in serving inputs or outcomes relative to the evaluated distribution; input divergence alone does not establish quality loss.
nodes.claim: Silent failure is made visible only by layered monitoring (infrastructure telemetry, input checks, label-free drift statistics, outcome metrics joined to matured labels), and confirmation speed is bounded by labeled-outcome arrival, so drift signals must route to an owner with a deadline.

nodes.label: Production monitoring
nodes.summary: Observation of infrastructure, input statistics, and model outcomes used to detect and diagnose production changes.
nodes.claim: Every production model runs detect, diagnose, decide, release, and recover, each step a control with a concrete machine cost, across three interfaces (data-model consistency, model-infrastructure parity, production feedback) where debt accumulates when a boundary erodes.

nodes.label: Rollback
nodes.summary: Recovery to a known-good artifact and configuration when a release violates operational bounds.
nodes.claim: A validated checkpoint is not yet a safe release: exposure is staged (shadow, canary, blue-green), every node is verified to run the intended version, and rollback is tiered, tested, and state-aware, because cached state survives a weights-only revert.

nodes.label: Subgroup fairness
nodes.summary: Declared error or decision-rate criteria measured across specified population slices and enforced at release.
nodes.claim: Disaggregated evaluation turns fairness into a release gate with per-slice demographic parity, equal opportunity, or equalized odds, criteria that cannot all hold under unequal base rates, so the criterion is a justified policy choice and each slice test returns pass, fail, or insufficient evidence.

nodes.label: Bias feedback
nodes.summary: A feedback mechanism in which model decisions alter future observations and training data, potentially amplifying disparity.
nodes.claim: When decisions censor future labels, disparity evolves geometrically across retraining intervals, so a gate passed at launch is a statement about the first interval, the feedback factor fitted from audits projects the breach, and randomized exploration is the serving cost that keeps it below one.

nodes.label: Operational carbon
nodes.summary: Emissions attributable to electricity use under a stated accounting boundary and electricity carbon intensity.
nodes.claim: Operational carbon is IT energy times PUE times grid carbon intensity, embodied carbon is a separate and sometimes majority term, and an optimization is responsible only if measured lifecycle energy and emissions fall for the same workload and quality target.

nodes.label: Operand transfer time
nodes.summary: Supplying operands takes time. For a fixed memory level, the transfer lower bound is bytes moved divided by bandwidth.

resources.title: The Roofline: predict and test the binding resource

nodes.claim: Attainable performance is the minimum of peak rate and bandwidth times arithmetic intensity, the ridge point (peak over bandwidth) marks where a kernel turns compute-bound, and intensity depends on implementation and batch, so the roofline bounds performance while profiling names the mechanism below the bound.

nodes.label: Arithmetic time
nodes.summary: The arithmetic lower bound is the required operations divided by the available compute rate. Faster operand delivery cannot remove this bound.

resources.title: The Roofline: predict and test the binding resource

nodes.claim: Attainable performance is the minimum of peak rate and bandwidth times arithmetic intensity, the ridge point (peak over bandwidth) marks where a kernel turns compute-bound, and intensity depends on implementation and batch, so the roofline bounds performance while profiling names the mechanism below the bound.

nodes.label: Memory bandwidth
nodes.summary: Bandwidth limits the rate at which an accelerator receives operands from a given memory level. The relevant level depends on data placement and reuse.
nodes.claim: Delivered throughput is set by where operands live, with registers and SRAM supplying the array at its rate while HBM, host memory over PCIe, and flash fall off a bandwidth taper, so the diagnostic is traffic across each boundary, not capacity alone.

nodes.label: Arithmetic intensity
nodes.summary: Operations per byte moved identifies the compute-versus-bandwidth regime. A suitable batch can reuse weights and raise this ratio.

resources.title: The Roofline: predict and test the binding resource

nodes.claim: Attainable performance is the minimum of peak rate and bandwidth times arithmetic intensity, the ridge point (peak over bandwidth) marks where a kernel turns compute-bound, and intensity depends on implementation and batch, so the roofline bounds performance while profiling names the mechanism below the bound.

nodes.label: Weight precision
nodes.summary: Lower precision reduces the bytes needed for weights. It improves runtime only when the execution regime and kernel support let those saved bytes matter.
nodes.claim: Fewer bits speed a compute-bound layer only through a faster integer datapath but speed a bandwidth-bound decode in proportion to bytes removed, and only when dequantization is fused into the matmul, so the same precision change gives different gains in different regimes.

nodes.label: Request latency
nodes.summary: The elapsed time from arrival to response includes waiting, host work, and model execution. The target applies to the complete request.
nodes.claim: End-to-end latency is a zero-sum budget spent serially on ingress, deserialization, preprocessing, transfer, queueing, inference, postprocessing, and egress and met at a stated quantile, so a faster model yields far less end-to-end gain when host stages dominate.

nodes.label: Queueing delay
nodes.summary: Requests wait when arrivals compete for busy resources. Near saturation, small increases in utilization can produce large increases in waiting.
nodes.claim: Little's law sizes the in-flight population and the M/M/1 model shows time in system rising nonlinearly with utilization, so capacity is sized as the utilization a percentile SLO permits, and under overload only admission control or graceful degradation preserve latency.

nodes.label: Batching
nodes.summary: Grouping requests shares fixed work and can reuse weights. It can improve capacity while adding formation delay; the useful batch is constrained by latency and memory.
nodes.claim: Batching amortizes fixed per-batch costs so saturated capacity grows almost linearly while fixed cost dominates, but every request pays formation delay, dynamic batching bounds it with a size-or-timeout trigger, and latency, memory, or the engine cap, not throughput, sets the largest useful batch.

nodes.label: Serving capacity
nodes.summary: Service capacity is the rate at which the system can complete work under a specified workload. The latency target constrains how much of that capacity can be used.
nodes.claim: Little's law sizes the in-flight population and the M/M/1 model shows time in system rising nonlinearly with utilization, so capacity is sized as the utilization a percentile SLO permits, and under overload only admission control or graceful degradation preserve latency.

nodes.label: Model weight memory
nodes.summary: Resident weights compete with KV state for device memory. Reducing weight storage can free cache capacity, subject to runtime allocations.
nodes.claim: After weights, remaining device memory divided by per-conversation cache bytes sets how many conversations one accelerator holds, so context length and batch trade against each other, and paged allocation, prefix caching, and offloading change that budget.

nodes.label: KV cache per conversation
nodes.summary: Attention keys and values retained for one conversation grow with its token count and model geometry.
nodes.claim: After weights, remaining device memory divided by per-conversation cache bytes sets how many conversations one accelerator holds, so context length and batch trade against each other, and paged allocation, prefix caching, and offloading change that budget.

nodes.label: Context length
nodes.summary: Longer histories retain more token state. At fixed cache format and model geometry, the per-conversation KV footprint grows linearly.
nodes.claim: After weights, remaining device memory divided by per-conversation cache bytes sets how many conversations one accelerator holds, so context length and batch trade against each other, and paged allocation, prefix caching, and offloading change that budget.

nodes.label: Decode
nodes.summary: Each generation step reads retained attention state and appends state for a new token.
nodes.claim: Token streaming splits latency into time to first token (prefill) and time per output token (decode), batching decode shares the weight stream but not cache reads, continuous batching reclaims slots as sequences end, and chunked prefill bounds the stall a long prompt imposes on active decodes.

nodes.label: Model execution time
nodes.summary: Execution includes arithmetic and moving operands. A resource bound gives a lower limit; profiling explains additional overhead.
nodes.claim: End-to-end latency is a zero-sum budget spent serially on ingress, deserialization, preprocessing, transfer, queueing, inference, postprocessing, and egress and met at a stated quantile, so a faster model yields far less end-to-end gain when host stages dominate.

nodes.label: Utilization
nodes.summary: Utilization compares offered work with available service capacity. High utilization leaves little room for variation in arrivals and execution.
nodes.claim: Little's law sizes the in-flight population and the M/M/1 model shows time in system rising nonlinearly with utilization, so capacity is sized as the utilization a percentile SLO permits, and under overload only admission control or graceful degradation preserve latency.

nodes.label: Batch formation delay
nodes.summary: A request may wait while the server collects a batch. This delay spends latency allowance before the model runs.
nodes.claim: Batching amortizes fixed per-batch costs so saturated capacity grows almost linearly while fixed cost dominates, but every request pays formation delay, dynamic batching bounds it with a size-or-timeout trigger, and latency, memory, or the engine cap, not throughput, sets the largest useful batch.

nodes.label: Available KV memory
nodes.summary: The device memory left after weights and other resident state bounds the cache pool.
nodes.claim: After weights, remaining device memory divided by per-conversation cache bytes sets how many conversations one accelerator holds, so context length and batch trade against each other, and paged allocation, prefix caching, and offloading change that budget.

nodes.label: Resident conversations
nodes.summary: Memory remaining after model weights must hold the attention state of every resident conversation.
nodes.claim: After weights, remaining device memory divided by per-conversation cache bytes sets how many conversations one accelerator holds, so context length and batch trade against each other, and paged allocation, prefix caching, and offloading change that budget.

nodes.label: Training batch size
nodes.summary: The number of training examples contributing to a parameter update; it affects execution efficiency and the updates required to reach target quality.
nodes.claim: In the macroscopic D·A·M product form of the iron law, training work is about 6PD FLOPs (D tokens times 6P FLOPs per token) and run time is that work over peak rate times utilization, so every point of utilization recovered at constant power removes time, energy, and dollars in the same proportion, while memory sits outside the law as a feasibility gate.
